name: Midface lift
lead: A midface lift is a cosmetic surgical procedure that repositions sagging cheek and lower-eyelid tissue upward, aiming to restore a fuller, younger-looking cheek, shorten the distance from the lower lid to the cheek and reduce the hollowed look beneath the eyes.[2][7][9] It is typically described as suited to patients in their 40s without marked jowling, with small incisions at the hairline and inside the mouth, and it can be combined with eyelid surgery.[1][2]

The operation grew out of facelift surgery. Early facelifts pulled skin sideways; later techniques lifted deeper layers, and reviewers describe a shift from lateral pulls toward more vertical vectors that rebuild the cheek and support the lower lid.[7][13] Techniques now include malar fat pad elevation, subperiosteal lifting, endoscopic approaches, transpalpebral approaches, suspension with absorbable devices, and high-SMAS facelift designs that reach the midface from a flap above the cheekbone.[3][6][9][10][13]

Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series, technique reviews and a small number of controlled studies, including a 2021 randomized trial of lift alone versus lift plus fat grafting.[7][14] Within looksmaxxing discussions it appears in patient reports of combined cheek and jaw implants, rhinoplasty and midface lift, and is also discussed as a surgical counterpart to filler and thread approaches to cheek volume.[12]

angle.text: A midface lift moves tissue that has slipped downward back over the cheekbone. People pursue it for a fuller malar area, less under-eye hollowing and a smoother line from lower lid to cheek.

paras: Wikipedia describes the midface lift as a facelift variant in which small incisions at the hairline and inside the mouth are used to lift the fat over the cheekbones. It names people in their 40s without significant jowling as suitable, and describes recovery as short.[2] The midface itself is described by Engle and colleagues as including the lower lid subunit and the cheek down to the nasolabial fold.[6]

The ageing changes that the procedure targets are descent of cheek fat, deepening nasolabial folds, tear-trough hollowing and changes at the lower lid.[2] In a 2006 review of the midface lift's history, Paul, Calvert and Evans wrote that the operation became popular because it can improve facial harmony by correcting midfacial atrophy, the tear trough deformity and the perceived malposition of the malar fat pad, concluding that conquering midface ageing is 'entirely related to vectors and volume'.[7]

Wikipedia places the first facelift in Berlin around 1901 by Eugen Holländer, with surgeons for most of the century pulling and trimming skin. Tord Skoog's subfacial dissection around 1970 and the 1976 description of the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) by Mitz and Peyronie, a term coined by Paul Tessier, moved surgery to deeper layers. Tessier's subperiosteal approach in the 1980s lifted soft tissue from the bone, and a volumetric period from the 1990s emphasised restoring lost volume and lifting upward.[2]

Reviews describe midface techniques evolving from approaches aimed at the lower face to ones aimed at the cheek and lower lid directly, since the midface lies outside the reach of classic lateral approaches.[7][13]

Malar fat pad elevation. De Cordier and colleagues reviewed 458 consecutive patients who had malar fat pad elevation between 1994 and 2000, with 472 midface lifts; the authors described the technique as effective with an acceptable complication rate and said facial nerve injury was infrequent and temporary.[9] Owsley and Zweifler described modifications based on the malar septum that reduced swelling and bruising, with patients usually returning to normal activities within 10 to 21 days.[15]

High SMAS. Marten's design places a flap along the superior border of the zygomatic arch and extends dissection medially so that jawline, cheek and midface are lifted together, without a separate midface procedure.[3]

Endoscopic and subperiosteal approaches. Engle and colleagues review endoscopic subperiosteal midface lifting and endoscopic malar fat pad lifting, alongside skin tightening by direct excision, skin-muscle flaps and fat pad transposition.[6] Sclafani and Dibelius describe the transpalpebral midface lift, reached through a lower-eyelid incision, as part of a shift toward centrofacial approaches that lift in more vertical vectors.[13]

Newer variants. A 2023 series by Bitik of 82 cases described intraorbital fixation, reporting that none of 58 primary patients developed ectropion or permanent lower eyelid malposition.[16] A 2024 series of 184 patients described a dual-plane midface and temporal lift through transoral and transtemporal routes, reporting improved P1/P2 ratio measurements.[17] A 2026 retrospective series of 42 patients described a subciliary three-vector technique, reporting lower lid-malar distance reduced by about 3.4 mm and 92.8 percent rating results as much or very much improved at 12 months.[18]

Threads and sutures. A 2006 prospective cohort of 10 women used an absorbable suspension device; nine showed significant aesthetic improvement, with one temporary zygomaticofacial nerve paresis.[19] A 2026 prospective case series of 84 patients combined lower blepharoplasty with barbed-thread midface suspension, with blinded raters judging perceived age about 7 years lower at 4 months, and the authors cautioned that follow-up was short.[18]

sections.h: Relation to eyelid surgery and non-surgical options
paras: Midface lifts are frequently paired with lower blepharoplasty. Wikipedia's blepharoplasty article lists fat repositioning and midface elevation as ways to smooth the transition from lower lid to cheek, together with canthopexy or canthoplasty to support the outer eyelid corner and fat transfer to restore periorbital volume.[5] Lower-lid support is a recurring concern in the literature, covered below.

A randomized trial by Barone and colleagues enrolled 56 patients (mean age 56.5) who had a primary subperiosteal midface lift and negative lower-eyelid vectors. Patients were randomized to lift alone or lift plus lipofilling; at about two years FACE-Q scores differed significantly between groups, the lift-and-fill group remained stable, and the lift-alone group had significantly more secondary procedures.[14]

Non-surgical approaches are discussed alongside. Registered trials include a 144-person study of hyaluronic acid-coated and non-coated threads for midface lifting (NCT07916103) and a 90-person study of hyaluronic acid fillers for midface volume deficiency (NCT03869450); Wikipedia's facelift article separately says thread lifts carry serious risks and that practitioners in the UK face minimal training requirements.[2][10][11]

Facelift-wide risks listed by Wikipedia include hematoma, the most common complication, nerve injury (the facial nerve being the most commonly injured motor nerve), skin necrosis, scarring, hair loss at temporal incisions and infection; smoking raises complication risk.[2]

For midface lifts and neighbouring eyelid surgery, the literature emphasises lower-lid position. A lower-blepharoplasty review addresses lid malposition and the role of lateral canthal support,[1] and a review of post-blepharoplasty lower eyelid retraction describes treatments including implants anchored at the orbital rim and hard palate grafts.[20] A study of 22 patients having endoscopic forehead/midface lifts found lower eyelid tension rose four- to five-fold immediately and remained about 1.7 to 1.9 times baseline at 12 months among the 15 patients still measured.[21] An 892-case review examined dry-eye symptoms and chemosis after blepharoplasty, including with a midface lift as an accompanying procedure.[4]

Published studies are mostly retrospective or technique reports rather than randomized trials, for example malar fat pad elevation case reviews and a 10-year follow-up of two sets of identical twins operated on by four surgeons using four techniques, critiqued at a surgical society meeting.[8][9] A 2026 systematic review of ten facelift randomized trials with 457 participants found average adherence to reporting guidelines of about 56 percent and concluded the evidence base is limited.[18] Registered trials of hyaluronic acid threads and fillers for midface volume or lifting exist but address non-surgical alternatives.[10][11]

Wikipedia gives facelift prices from about US$2,500 in India and Panama to US$15,000 in the US and Canada as of 2008, with 2009 European costs of roughly 4,000 to 9,000 pounds; it describes these as dated, and prices vary by surgeon and country.[2] Facelifts were the third most popular US aesthetic surgery in 2019, behind rhinoplasty and blepharoplasty.[2]

A looksmax.org thread presents a patient's combined cheek, chin, jaw implant, rhinoplasty and midface lift result from a surgeon overseas, with the poster describing travelling from Australia and reporting being very satisfied seven months after surgery; community reaction focused on the overall change.[12]

Cheek fullness and under-eye support are among the facial features valued in looksmaxxing vocabulary, where hollow or flat midface areas are a common topic. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists facial surgery among hardmaxxing practices.[22]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, midface lifts appear mainly in surgery-result posts from patients who combined them with implants and nose surgery, and in discussion of cheek and under-eye hollowing.[12]

claims.claim: A midface lift can restore cheek fullness and fix under-eye hollowing
claims.believers: Patients sharing results describe being very satisfied after combined cheek, jaw and nose surgery with a midface lift.[12]
claims.experts: Surgical series report improved midface volume scores and patient ratings, mostly in case series; a randomized trial found higher satisfaction when lipofilling was added.[14][16]

claims.claim: Combining the lift with fat grafting gives longer-lasting results
claims.believers: Surgeons and patients describe lift-and-fill as a way to rebuild volume as well as position.[14]
claims.experts: In the 56-patient randomized trial, the lift-and-fill group remained stable and needed fewer secondary procedures at about two years.[14]

claims.claim: Threads and fillers can replace surgery for cheek lifting
claims.believers: Practitioners offer thread and filler options as shorter-recovery alternatives.[10][11]
claims.experts: Trials are registered for threads and hyaluronic acid fillers, and Wikipedia says thread lifts carry serious risks; a 2026 case series reported minor complications with thread suspension.[2][10][11][18]

claims.claim: Lower-eyelid complications are a risk of the procedure
claims.believers: Surgeons describe fixation and canthal support techniques to avoid lid malposition.[16]
claims.experts: Reviews address lid malposition and retraction after related surgery, and a prospective study found lower eyelid tension remained above baseline at 12 months.[1][20][21]

card.summary: Surgery that lifts sagging cheek tissue; established in facial plastic surgery but backed mostly by surgeon case series.
card.aka: Cheek lift; malar fat pad elevation
card.note: Surgical risks include lid malposition and dry eye reported around related procedures.

quick.overview:
A midface lift raises cheek and lower-eyelid tissue to restore volume and reduce hollowing. It is often discussed for people in their 40s and is frequently combined with eyelid surgery.

Evidence comes mainly from surgeon case series and technique reviews.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons elevate and resuspend midface soft tissue, via approaches such as the malar fat pad or high SMAS flap, through incisions near the hairline, eyelid or mouth.
quick.risks: Reported complications in related eyelid and facelift surgery include lid malposition and dry-eye symptoms. It is major surgery performed by trained surgeons.
